claim: Photoreceptors from the eye-disc induce their target field, the lamina, such that for every unit eye there is a corresponding lamina unit (column).
source: Photoreceptors from the eye-disc induce their target field, the lamina, such that for every unit eye there is a corresponding lamina unit (column).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is consistent with established knowledge about Drosophila visual system development.

claim: Each lamina column initially contains approximately 6 post-mitotic lamina precursors.
source: Although each column initially contains ~6 post-mitotic lamina precursors, only 5 differentiate into neurons, called L1-L5
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by the schematic in Figure 1A.

claim: Only 5 lamina precursors differentiate into neurons (L1-L5) in each column.
source: Although each column initially contains ~6 post-mitotic lamina precursors, only 5 differentiate into neurons, called L1-L5
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The 'extra' precursor is invariantly positioned above the L5 neuron in each column.
source: the 'extra' precursor, which is invariantly positioned above the L5 neuron in each column, undergoes apoptosis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by imaging data showing Dcp-1 positive cells in specific positions.

claim: The 'extra' precursor undergoes apoptosis.
source: the 'extra' precursor, which is invariantly positioned above the L5 neuron in each column, undergoes apoptosis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Dcp-1 staining data in Figure 2.

claim: The outer chiasm giant glia (xgO) reside below the lamina.
source: a glial population called the outer chiasm giant glia (xgO), which resides below the lamina
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: xgO secrete multiple ligands to induce L5 differentiation in response to epidermal growth factor (EGF) from photoreceptors.
source: a glial population called the outer chiasm giant glia (xgO), which resides below the lamina, secretes multiple ligands to induce L5 differentiation in response to epidermal growth factor (EGF) from photoreceptors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing rescue experiments with Spi and Col4a1.

claim: The 'extra' precursor is specified as an L5.
source: We found that the row of precursors nearest to xgO differentiate into L5s and, in turn, antagonise differentiation signalling to prevent the 'extra' precursors from differentiating, resulting in their death. Thus, an intricate interplay of glial signals and feedback from differentiating neurons defines an invariant and stereotyped pattern of neuronal differentiation and programmed cell death to ensure that lamina columns each contain exactly one L5 neuron.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4 showing ectopic L5s when differentiation is forced.

claim: Two precursors are specified as L5s but only one differentiates during normal development.
source: Therefore, two precursors are specified as L5s but only one differentiates during normal development.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing ectopic L5 differentiation when MAPK is hyperactivated.

claim: The row of precursors nearest to xgO differentiate into L5s.
source: We found that the row of precursors nearest to xgO differentiate into L5s
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the tissue architecture and experimental observations.

claim: Newly induced L5s antagonise differentiation signalling to prevent the 'extra' precursors from differentiating.
source: We found that the row of precursors nearest to xgO differentiate into L5s and, in turn, antagonise differentiation signalling to prevent the 'extra' precursors from differentiating, resulting in their death.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5 showing Argos expression and RNAi experiments.

claim: Neuronal numbers can be set by controlling how many progeny a neural stem cell produces.
source: Neuronal numbers can be set by controlling how many progeny a neural stem cell produces, or by regulating how many neural progeny survive (Hidalgo and ffrench-Constant, 2003; Miguel-Aliaga and Thor, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Neuronal numbers can be set by regulating how many neural progeny survive.
source: Neuronal numbers can be set by controlling how many progeny a neural stem cell produces, or by regulating how many neural progeny survive (Hidalgo and ffrench-Constant, 2003; Miguel-Aliaga and Thor, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The fly visual system is organised retinotopically into repeated modular circuits.
source: Like vertebrate visual systems, the fly visual system is organised retinotopically into repeated modular circuits that process sensory input from unique points in space spanning the entire visual field (Hadjieconomou et al., 2011; Malin and Desplan, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Photoreceptors are born progressively in the eye imaginal disc as a wave of differentiation sweeps across the tissue from posterior to anterior.
source: Photoreceptors are born progressively in the eye imaginal disc as a wave of differentiation sweeps across the tissue from posterior to anterior.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is consistent with established knowledge about Drosophila eye development.

claim: Newly born photoreceptors express Hedgehog (Hh), which promotes further wave propagation.
source: Newly born photoreceptors express Hedgehog (Hh), which promotes further wave propagation (Treisman, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Photoreceptors express the epidermal growth factor (EGF), Spitz (Spi), which recruits additional photoreceptors into developing ommatidia.
source: They also express the epidermal growth factor (EGF), Spitz (Spi), which recruits additional photoreceptors into developing ommatidia (Treisman, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Photoreceptor axons project into the optic lobe and induce the lamina.
source: As photoreceptors are born, their axons project into the optic lobe and induce the lamina, such that there is a corresponding lamina unit (or cartridge) for every ommatidium (Figure 1A; Hadjieconomou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation and Figure 1A schematic.

claim: Each lamina cartridge is composed of five interneurons (L1-L5) and multiple glial subtypes.
source: Each cartridge is composed of five interneurons (L1-L5; named for the medulla layers they project to) and multiple glial subtypes (Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989; Hadjieconomou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Photoreceptor-derived Hh converts neuroepithelial cells into lamina precursor cells (LPCs).
source: Photoreceptor-derived Hh converts neuroepithelial cells into lamina precursor cells (LPCs), promotes their terminal divisions and drives the assembly of lamina pre-cartridges referred to as columns, that is, ensembles of ~6 post-mitotic LPCs stacked together and associated with photoreceptor axon bundles (Figure 1A and B; Huang and Kunes, 1998; Huang and Kunes, 1996; Sugie et al., 2010; Umetsu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations and Figure 1A and B.

claim: Photoreceptor-derived Hh promotes terminal divisions of LPCs.
source: Photoreceptor-derived Hh converts neuroepithelial cells into lamina precursor cells (LPCs), promotes their terminal divisions and drives the assembly of lamina pre-cartridges referred to as columns, that is, ensembles of ~6 post-mitotic LPCs stacked together and associated with photoreceptor axon bundles (Figure 1A and B; Huang and Kunes, 1998; Huang and Kunes, 1996; Sugie et al., 2010; Umetsu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Photoreceptor-derived Hh drives the assembly of lamina columns.
source: Photoreceptor-derived Hh converts neuroepithelial cells into lamina precursor cells (LPCs), promotes their terminal divisions and drives the assembly of lamina pre-cartridges referred to as columns, that is, ensembles of ~6 post-mitotic LPCs stacked together and associated with photoreceptor axon bundles (Figure 1A and B; Huang and Kunes, 1998; Huang and Kunes, 1996; Sugie et al., 2010; Umetsu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: LPCs are diversified by graded Hh signalling along the distal-proximal axis of young columns.
source: Once assembled into columns, LPCs are diversified by graded Hh signalling along the distal-proximal axis of young columns (Bostock et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: LPCs differentiate into neurons following an invariant spatio-temporal pattern whereby the most proximal and most distal cells differentiate first into L5 and L2, respectively.
source: They then differentiate into neurons following an invariant spatio-temporal pattern whereby the most proximal (bottom) and most distal (top) cells differentiate first into L5 and L2, respectively; differentiation then proceeds in a distal-to-proximal (top-to-bottom) sequence, L3 forming next, followed by L1, then L4 (Fernandes et al., 2017; Huang et al., 1998; Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Differentiation proceeds in a distal-to-proximal sequence: L3, then L1, then L4.
source: differentiation then proceeds in a distal-to-proximal (top-to-bottom) sequence, L3 forming next, followed by L1, then L4 (Fernandes et al., 2017; Huang et al., 1998; Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The sixth LPC, located between L4 and L5, does not differentiate but is fated to die by apoptosis.
source: The sixth LPC, located between L4 and L5, does not differentiate but instead is fated to die by apoptosis and is later cleared (Figure 1A; Apitz and Salecker, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation and Figure 1A.

claim: Wrapping glia ensheathe photoreceptor axons.
source: This spatio-temporal pattern of neuronal differentiation is driven in part by a population of glia called wrapping glia, which ensheathes photoreceptor axons and which induces L1-L4 neuronal differentiation via insulin/insulin-like growth factor signalling in response to EGF from photoreceptors (Fernandes et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Wrapping glia induce L1-L4 neuronal differentiation via insulin/insulin-like growth factor signalling in response to EGF from photoreceptors.
source: This spatio-temporal pattern of neuronal differentiation is driven in part by a population of glia called wrapping glia, which ensheathes photoreceptor axons and which induces L1-L4 neuronal differentiation via insulin/insulin-like growth factor signalling in response to EGF from photoreceptors (Fernandes et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: L1-L4 neuronal differentiation can be disrupted by manipulating wrapping glia without affecting L5 differentiation.
source: Intriguingly, L1-L4 neuronal differentiation can be disrupted by manipulating wrapping glia without affecting L5 differentiation (Fernandes et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Blocking EGFR signalling in all glia results in a complete block in lamina neuron differentiation.
source: Although LPCs (Dac+ cells) still formed and assembled into columns, there was a complete block in lamina neuron differentiation as seen by the absence of the pan-neuronal marker, Embryonic lethal abnormal vision (Elav); that is, L5 differentiation was disrupted in addition to the differentiation of L1-L4 as expected (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: EGFR activity in a glial population other than wrapping glia is required for L5 neuronal differentiation.
source: Thus, EGFR activity in a glial population other than the wrapping glia is required for L5 neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is inferred from the experimental data showing that blocking EGFR in all glia affects L5 differentiation.

claim: Blocking EGFR signalling in xgO leads to a dramatic reduction in the number of L5s.
source: Therefore, we performed a screen using glia subtype-specific Gal4s to block EGFR signalling and determined what effect this manipulation had on L5s using Elav expression in the proximal lamina (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-M; summarised in Supplementary file 1). Blocking EGFR signalling in the xgO led to a dramatic reduction in the number of L5s (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Blocking EGFR signalling in xgO from the third larval instar results in a loss of Elav positive cells in the proximal lamina.
source: To rule out early developmental defects, we used a temperature-sensitive Gal80 (Gal80ts) and shifted animals from the permissive temperature to the restrictive temperature to limit EGFRDN expression in xgO to begin from the third larval instar, when lamina development initiates. This resulted in a similar loss of Elav positive cells in the proximal lamina as when EGFRDN was expressed continuously in the xgO, indicating that this phenotype is not due to an early defect in xgO (Figure 1—figure supplement 1N).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1N.

claim: Blocking EGFR signalling in xgO does not affect xgO numbers or morphology.
source: Importantly, blocking EGFR signalling in the xgO did not affect xgO numbers or morphology (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1O-R).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1E, F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1O-R.

claim: Blocking EGFR activity in xgO specifically decreases the number of L5 neurons while other lamina neuron types are unaffected.
source: We found that the number of L5 neurons decreased specifically, while the number of all the other neuron types were unaffected (Figure 1G–I; pL5 <0.0001, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1G-I.

claim: L5s are mostly absent in the adult lamina when EGFR is blocked in xgO.
source: Similar to our results in the developing lamina, L5s were mostly absent in the adult lamina when EGFR was blocked in xgO compared with controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1S, T; Nexp = 10; Nctrl = 11), indicating that the loss of L5s observed during development is not due to delayed induction.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1S, T.

claim: EGFR activity in xgO is required for L5 neuronal differentiation.
source: Thus, EGFR activity in xgO is required for L5 neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: LPC formation and column assembly occur normally when EGFR is blocked in xgO.
source: In columns 1–4, there were no differences in the number of LPCs when EGFR was blocked in xgO, indicating that LPC formation and column assembly occurred normally (Figure 2C), supporting the hypothesis that in response to EGFR activity, xgO induce proximal LPCs to differentiate as L5s.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The number of LPCs begins to decrease in older columns (column 5 onwards) when EGFR signalling is blocked in xgO.
source: Interestingly, the number of LPCs began to decrease in older columns (column 5 onwards) when EGFR signalling was blocked in xgO (Figure 2C; *p<0.05, ***p<0.0002, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There is a significant increase in the number of Dcp-1 positive cells in the lamina when EGFR signalling is blocked in xgO.
source: We used an antibody against the cleaved form of Death caspase-1 (Dcp-1), an effector caspase, to detect apoptotic cells (Akagawa et al., 2015) and, indeed, observed a significant increase in the number of Dcp-1 positive cells in the lamina when EGFR signalling was blocked in the xgO (132.8 cells/unit volume±19.48 standard error of the mean) compared to controls (49.14 cells/unit volume±4.53) (Figure 2A–B and D, p<0.0005, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2A-B and D.

claim: Dcp-1 positive cells are observed in the proximal row of the lamina when EGFR signalling is blocked in xgO, which is never observed in controls.
source: Importantly, we observed Dcp-1 positive cells in the proximal row of the lamina (Figure 2B; Nexp = 20/20), which we never observed in controls (Figure 2A, Nctrl = 19/19).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: EGFR activity in xgO induces the differentiation of L5 neurons, and proximal LPCs that fail to receive appropriate cues from xgO die by apoptosis.
source: Altogether these results showed that EGFR activity in xgO induces the differentiation of L5 neurons, and proximal LPCs that fail to receive appropriate cues from xgO die by apoptosis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Photoreceptor-derived EGF is required for L5 differentiation.
source: We took advantage of a mutant for rhomboid 3 (rho3) in which photoreceptors are specified but cannot secrete EGF from their axons (Yogev et al., 2010), resulting in failure of L1-L4 neurons to differentiate along with a significant decrease in the number of L5s (Figure 3A and C; prho3 <0.0001; one-way ANOVA with Dunn's multiple comparisons test) (Fernandes et al., 2017; Yogev et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3A and C using rho3 mutants.

claim: Restoring Rho3 expression only in photoreceptors in rho3 mutant animals fully rescues L5 neuronal differentiation.
source: To test this hypothesis, we restored expression of wild-type Rho3 only in photoreceptors in rho3 mutant animals using a photoreceptor-specific driver (GMR-Gal4). Rho3 function in photoreceptors was sufficient to fully rescue not only L1-L4 neuronal differentiation, as previously reported (Yogev et al., 2010), but also L5 neuronal differentiation (Figure 3B and C; one-way ANOVA with Dunn's multiple comparisons test).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: xgO likely respond to EGF from photoreceptors and relay these signals to induce differentiation of proximal LPCs into L5 neurons.
source: Since photoreceptor-derived EGF was insufficient to induce L5 neuronal differentiation when EGFR signalling was blocked in xgO (Figure 1F and H), together these results suggest that xgO likely respond to EGF from photoreceptors and relay these signals to induce differentiation of proximal LPCs into L5 neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: Blocking EGFR signalling in xgO leads to reduced levels of double phosphorylated MAPK (dpMAPK) specifically in the proximal lamina.
source: Previously, we showed that MAPK signalling is necessary and sufficient for neuronal differentiation in the lamina (Fernandes et al., 2017). Therefore, we reasoned that xgO-derived differentiation signal(s) must activate MAPK signalling through a receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) in the proximal lamina. Indeed, blocking EGFR signalling in xgO led to reduced levels of double phosphorylated MAPK (dpMAPK) specifically in the proximal lamina (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Co-expressing PntP1 with EGFRDN in xgO rescues the number of L5s per column.
source: To validate this approach, we tested whether autonomously restoring transcriptional activity downstream of MAPK in xgO while blocking EGFR activity could rescue L5 differentiation. While blocking EGFR in xgO resulted in laminas containing 0.063±0.014 L5s per column, co-expressing PntP1 with EGFRDN in xgO rescued the number of L5s per column to 0.213±0.025 (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C ****p<0.0001 compared to EGFRDN alone).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Spi, Branchless (Bnl), Thisbe (Ths), and Col4a1 produced statistically significant rescues of L5 differentiation when co-expressed with EGFRDN in xgO.
source: We then screened 18 RTK ligands based on available reagents (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C). Four ligands, Spi, Branchless (Bnl), Thisbe (Ths), and Col4a1, produced statistically significant rescues when compared with the xgO>EGFRDN + CD8::GFP (Gal4 titration control) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C; *p<0.05, **p<0.005, ***p<0.0005, ****p<0.0001 one-way ANOVA with Dunn's multiple comparisons test).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: bnl-Gal4 drives expression in all cells of the optic lobe.
source: Using a previously validated bnl-Gal4 (Chen and Krasnow, 2014; Kamimura et al., 2006; Spéder and Brand, 2014; Tamamouna et al., 2021), we drove CD8::GFP expression and found that it was expressed in all cells of the optic lobe (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), making it unlikely to be a viable hit.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ths-Gal4 drives expression in photoreceptors but not xgO.
source: We found that a previously validated ths-Gal4 (Anllo and DiNardo, 2022; Wu et al., 2017) drove CD8::GFP expression in photoreceptors but not xgO (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) consistent with previous reports (Franzdóttir et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and citations.

claim: Col4a1-Gal4 drives expression in xgO.
source: However, when we examined Col4a1 expression using a previously validated Gal4 enhancer trap (Hennig et al., 2006), we found that it drove CD8::GFP expression in xgO (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: spi-Gal4 (NP0289-Gal4) drives expression in xgO.
source: We also found that a spi-Gal4 (NP0289-Gal4; not previously validated) drove CD8::GFP expression in xgO, but not photoreceptors or other cell types where spi is also known to be expressed, suggesting that this Gal4 line may report spi expression partially (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: spi and Col4a1 mRNAs are present in xgO under physiological conditions.
source: To further substantiate these results we performed fluorescence in situ hybridisation chain reaction (HCR), a form of fluorescent in situ hybridisation (Choi et al., 2018; Choi et al., 2016; Duckhorn et al., 2022), and confirmed that spi and Col4a1 mRNAs were present in the xgO under physiological conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and I; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by in situ HCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and I.

claim: Spi and Col4a1 rescued L5 differentiation when co-expressed with EGFRDN in xgO.
source: This enabled us to narrow down our hits to two ligands: the EGF Spi and Col4a1, a type IV Collagen, which both rescued L5 differentiation resulting in laminas with 0.147±0.024 and 0.17±0.0197 L5s per column, respectively (Figure 3F–K and P pspi-wt <0.01 and pCol4a1 <0.0005, one-way ANOVA with Dunn's multiple comparisons test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3F-K and P.

claim: xgO are capable of processing mSpi into the active form (sSpi).
source: Note that expressing either sSpi or wild-type (unprocessed) mSpi (referred to as Spiwt) in xgO rescued L5 numbers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), indicating that xgO are capable of processing mSpi into the active form (sSpi).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Spi expression in xgO does not autonomously rescue dpMAPK nuclear localisation in xgO when EGFR signalling is blocked.
source: We ruled out the trivial explanation that the rescue of L5 numbers by Spi was caused by autocrine EGFR reactivation in the xgO, as Spi expression in xgO did not autonomously rescue dpMAPK nuclear localisation in xgO when EGFR signalling was blocked (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B, J, K).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B, J, K.

claim: Disrupting EGFR signalling in xgO results in significantly reduced fluorescence signal for spi and Col4a1 transcripts in xgO.
source: We measured spi and Col4a1 transcript levels using in situ HCR in controls and when we blocked EGFR signalling in xgO. Disrupting EGFR signalling in xgO resulted in a significantly reduced fluorescence signal for spi and Col4a1 transcripts in xgO compared with controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and I, 1L-O; pspi <0.01, pCol4a1<0.005; Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H, I, L-O.

claim: xgO express spi and Col4a1 in response to EGFR activity.
source: Thus, xgO express spi and Col4a1 in response to EGFR activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Ddr-Gal4 drives expression in all LPCs.
source: We used a Gal4 enhancer trap in the Ddr locus (not previously validated) to drive CD8::GFP expression and observed that GFP was expressed in all LPCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1P).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1P.

claim: Ddr is expressed throughout the lamina.
source: We confirmed these results using in situ HCR, which also detected Ddr expression throughout the lamina (Figure 3—figure supplement 1Q).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by in situ HCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1Q.

claim: LPCs express the RTKs that make them competent to respond to Spi and Col4a1 produced by xgO.
source: Spi activates EGFR (Sopko and Perrimon, 2013), which was shown to be expressed in LPCs previously (Huang et al., 1998). Thus, LPCs express the RTKs that make them competent to respond to the EGF Spi and Col4a1 produced by xgO.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is inferred from the expression patterns and previous literature.

claim: Expressing spi or Col4a1 in xgO in which EGFR signalling was blocked rescued dpMAPK signal in L5s.
source: Moreover, expressing spi or Col4a1 in xgO in which EGFR signalling was blocked rescued dpMAPK signal in L5s, indicating that, when expressed in xgO, these ligands were sufficient to activate MAPK signalling in the proximal lamina (Figure 3—figure supplement 1R-T; **p<0.005, ****p<0.0001; one-way ANOVA with Dunn's multiple comparisons test).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1R-T.

claim: Co-expressing Spi and Col4a1 in xgO>EGFRDN background led to an enhanced rescue of L5 differentiation relative to individual ligand rescues.
source: Co-expressing Spi and Col4a1 in the xgO>EGFRDN background led to an enhanced and statistically significant rescue relative to individual ligand rescues alone, resulting in laminas with 0.267±0.025 L5s per column (Figure 3L–P; p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3L-P.

claim: Overexpressing Spi in xgO results in a 19%±1.8 increase in the number of L5s per column relative to controls.
source: We also tested whether these ligands could induce ectopic L5 differentiation when overexpressed in the xgO. Overexpressing either Spi or Col4a1 resulted in a 19%±1.8 (p<0.05) and a 24%±4 (p<0.005) increase in the number of L5s per column relative to controls, respectively (Figure 3Q–S).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3Q-S.

claim: Overexpressing Col4a1 in xgO results in a 24%±4 increase in the number of L5s per column relative to controls.
source: Overexpressing either Spi or Col4a1 resulted in a 19%±1.8 (p<0.05) and a 24%±4 (p<0.005) increase in the number of L5s per column relative to controls, respectively (Figure 3Q–S).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3Q-S.

claim: Spi and Col4a1 from xgO are sufficient to induce L5 differentiation.
source: Thus, Spi and Col4a1 from xgO are sufficient to induce L5 differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the overexpression experiments.

claim: Knocking down Col4a1 in xgO leads to a statistically significant decrease in L5s.
source: We used RNA interference (RNAi) to knock down spi and Col4a1 expression both individually and simultaneously in xgO using previously validated lines (Chen et al., 2016; Csordás et al., 2020; Louradour et al., 2017; Morante et al., 2013; Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011). While knocking down spi led to a mild decrease in L5 numbers, which was not statistically significant, knocking down Col4a1 in the xgO led to a statistically significant decrease in L5s (0.78±0.03 L5s per column) relative to controls (0.92±0.02 L5s per column) (Figure 3T, U and W; *p<0.05 one-way ANOVA with Dunn's multiple comparisons test).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3T, U and W.

claim: Knocking down both spi and Col4a1 simultaneously in xgO leads to a strong decrease in L5s.
source: However, knocking down both spi and Col4a1 simultaneously in xgO led to a strong decrease in L5s (0.61±0.02 L5s per column; Figure 3V–W; ****p<0.0001, one-way ANOVA with Dunn's multiple comparisons test).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3V-W.

claim: Dcp-1 positive apoptotic cells are observed in the most proximal row of the lamina when both spi and Col4a1 are knocked down in xgO.
source: Under these conditions we also observed Dcp-1 positive apoptotic cells in the most proximal row of the lamina, which were never observed in controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) but were observed when L5 differentiation was blocked above (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: xgO-derived Spi and Col4a1 are both necessary and sufficient to induce L5 differentiation.
source: Thus, xgO-derived Spi and Col4a1 are both necessary and sufficient to induce L5 differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the RNAi and overexpression experiments.

claim: xgO secrete multiple factors that lead to activation of the MAPK cascade in the proximal lamina to induce differentiation of L5s.
source: Altogether, we found that xgO secrete multiple factors that lead to activation of the MAPK cascade in the proximal lamina to induce differentiation of L5s.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: A gradient of Hh signalling activity in lamina columns specifies L1-L5 identities such that high levels specify L2 and L3 identities, intermediate levels specify L1 and L4 identities, and low levels specify L5 identity.
source: We recently showed that a gradient of Hh signalling activity in lamina columns specifies L1-L5 identities such that high levels specify L2 and L3 (distal cell) identities, intermediate levels specify L1 and L4 (intermediate cell) identities, and low levels specify L5 (proximal cell) identity (Bostock et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Overexpressing spi and Col4a1 in xgO results in ectopic L5 neurons.
source: Since overexpressing spi and Col4a1 in the xgO resulted in ectopic L5 neurons, we wondered what the source of these ectopic cells was.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the experimental observations.

claim: There is no decrease in the number of L1-L3s or L4s per column when either spi or Col4a1 is overexpressed in xgO.
source: We quantified other lamina neuron types when either spi or Col4a1 was overexpressed in xgO and found no decrease in the number of L1-L3s (Slp2-only expressing cells) or L4s (Bsh-only expressing cells) per column compared to controls (Figure 3S).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3S.

claim: Ectopic L5s are not produced at the expense of other lamina neuron types.
source: Thus, ectopic L5s were not produced at the expense of other lamina neuron types.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the quantification data.

claim: The 'extra' LPCs are specified with L5 identity through low Hh signalling activity in the proximal lamina.
source: We hypothesised that though fated to die, 'extra' LPCs are specified with L5 identity through low Hh signalling activity in the proximal lamina, and that the overexpression of Spi and Col4a1 in xgO generated ectopic L5s by inducing differentiation and survival of the 'extra' LPCs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a hypothesis based on previous findings and current observations.

claim: Hyperactivating MAPK signalling in the lamina leads to premature neuronal differentiation.
source: As reported previously, hyperactivating MAPK signalling in the lamina led to premature neuronal differentiation: instead of sequential differentiation of L1-L4, seen as a triangular front, most lamina columns differentiated simultaneously ( (Figure 4) , Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, C; Fernandes et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, C, as well as a citation.

claim: No LPCs remain undifferentiated past lamina column 5 when MAPK signalling is hyperactivated, including the row of cells that normally correspond to the 'extra' LPCs.
source: We observed no LPCs that remained undifferentiated (Dac+ and Elav-) past lamina column 5, including the row of cells that normally correspond to the 'extra' LPCs (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, C.

claim: There is a concomitant decrease in cleaved Dcp-1 positive cells when MAPK signalling is hyperactivated in the lamina.
source: Importantly, we also observed a concomitant decrease in cleaved Dcp-1 positive cells (Figure 4C and E ; p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney U-test), suggesting that forcing the 'extra' LPCs to differentiate blocked their death.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4C and E.

claim: Forcing the 'extra' LPCs to differentiate blocks their death.
source: Importantly, we also observed a concomitant decrease in cleaved Dcp-1 positive cells (Figure 4C and E ; p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney U-test), suggesting that forcing the 'extra' LPCs to differentiate blocked their death.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: Two rows of cells co-expressing Slp2 and Bsh are often observed in the proximal lamina when neuronal differentiation is forced.
source: Next, we examined the distribution of lamina neuron types when we forced neuronal differentiation. We often observed two rows of cells co-expressing Slp2 and Bsh in the proximal lamina (Figure 4B and D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, D), indicating the presence of ectopic L5s.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B, D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, D.

claim: The average number of L5s per column is approximately 1.4-fold higher in laminas in which differentiation is ectopically induced compared with controls.
source: While there was no significant difference between the average number of L1-L3s or L4s per column, the average number of L5s per column was ~1.4-fold higher in laminas in which differentiation was ectopically induced compared with controls, that is, they contained 1.4±0.08 L5s per column compared to 1.00±0.05 L5s per column in controls (Figure 4B, D and F–G; p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4B, D and F-G.

claim: Hyperactivating MAPK signalling in the lamina drives ectopic differentiation of L5 neurons.
source: Thus, hyperactivating MAPK signalling in the lamina drove ectopic differentiation of L5 neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Ectopic L5s are only observed in the proximal but never in the distal lamina when MAPK signalling is hyperactivated.
source: Importantly, ectopic L5s were only observed in the proximal but never in the distal lamina (Figure 4D, N=18/18; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, N=9/9).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The absence of cell death in the row distal to L5s and the presence of ectopic L5s in this row indicate that hyperactivating MAPK signalling induces the 'extra' LPCs to differentiate into L5s.
source: Taken together, the absence of cell death in the row distal to L5s and the presence of ectopic L5s in this row indicate that hyperactivating MAPK signalling induces the 'extra' LPCs to differentiate into L5s.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The 'extra' LPCs are specified as L5s though fated to die normally.
source: Thus, the 'extra' LPCs are specified as L5s though fated to die normally.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Lamina precursors are specified by Hh signalling prior to differentiation.
source: These data are consistent with our work showing that lamina precursors are specified by Hh signalling prior to differentiation and that the most proximal cells, which experience the lowest levels of Hh pathway activity and are specified as L5s (Bostock et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: More LPCs are specified as L5s than differentiate normally.
source: Importantly, the presence of ectopic L5s when differentiation is induced demonstrates that more LPCs are specified as L5s than differentiate normally.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Cleaved Dcp-1 is absent in homozygous DroncI24 animals, confirming that apoptosis is blocked.
source: We tested whether the 'extra' LPCs differentiated as L5s when apoptosis was blocked in animals mutant for Death regulator Nedd2-like caspase (Dronc), an initiator caspase essential for caspase-dependent cell death (Fuchs and Steller, 2011). Cleaved Dcp-1 was absent in homozygous DroncI24 animals confirming that apoptosis was blocked (Figure 5A; N=26/26; with full penetrance).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cells that are positive for Dac but negative for Elav are detected between L1-L4 and L5 neurons past column 5 in DroncI24 animals, which are never observed in controls.
source: Indeed, we detected cells that were positive for the lamina marker Dachshund (Dac) but negative for the pan-neuronal marker Elav between L1-L4 and L5 neurons past column 5, which were never observed in controls (Figure 5A compared to Figure 4A; N=13/13; with full penetrance).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5A compared to Figure 4A.

claim: The 'extra' LPCs retained when apoptosis is blocked do not express lamina neuron-type markers Slp2 or Bsh.
source: These cells did not express lamina neuron-type markers Slp2 or Bsh, which L5s co-express and which individually label L1-L3s and L4s, respectively (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Although the 'extra' LPCs are retained when apoptosis is blocked, they do not differentiate into neurons.
source: Thus, although the 'extra' LPCs were retained when apoptosis was blocked, they did not differentiate into neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Ectopic L5s are observed only when all LPCs are forced to differentiate, bypassing the need for differentiation signals from glia, but not when apoptosis is blocked.
source: We observed ectopic L5s only when all LPCs were forced to differentiate, bypassing the need for differentiation signals from glia, but not when apoptosis was blocked (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D, and Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from comparing different experimental conditions.

claim: The 'extra' LPCs, though specified as L5s, do not receive differentiation signals from xgO in Dronc mutants or in the wild-type.
source: This suggests that the 'extra' LPCs, though specified as L5s, did not receive differentiation signals from xgO in Dronc mutants or in the wild-type, where failing to differentiate they were eliminated by apoptosis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: The most proximal row of LPCs fated to differentiate into L5s is the row nearest to xgO, and therefore, the first to receive differentiation signals.
source: How are only half of the LPCs specified as L5s chosen to differentiate in an invariant manner? The most proximal row of LPCs fated to differentiate into L5s is the row nearest to xgO, and therefore, the first to receive differentiation signals.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is inferred from the tissue architecture.

claim: Newly induced L5s may limit the ability of more distal LPCs to differentiate by preventing MAPK activation in neighbouring cells.
source: We speculated that newly induced L5s may then limit the ability of more distal LPCs to differentiate, by preventing MAPK activation in neighbouring cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a speculation based on the observations.

claim: Argos (Aos) is a transcriptional target of MAPK signalling and a secreted antagonist of the EGF Spi.
source: Aos is a transcriptional target of MAPK signalling and a secreted antagonist of the EGF Spi (Freeman et al., 1992; Golembo et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: aos-lacZ is expressed in xgO and differentiating lamina neurons, with the highest levels detected in L5s.
source: To test this hypothesis, we examined argos (aos) expression with an enhancer trap in the aos locus, aosW11. aos-lacZ (aosW11/+) was expressed in xgO and differentiating lamina neurons, with the highest levels detected in L5s (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: Ectopic L5s are noted in the laminas of aosW11 heterozygotes.
source: Interestingly, we also noted ectopic L5s in the laminas of aosW11 heterozygotes, which could be the result of decreased Aos expression, as aosW11 is a hypomorphic loss-of-function allele (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Knocking down aos in developing L5s results in a statistically significant approximately 1.2-fold increase in the number of L5s relative to controls.
source: To test this hypothesis, we knocked down aos by RNAi using a driver expressed specifically in developing L5s (Jenett et al., 2012; Figure 5G). We observed a statistically significant ~1.2-fold increase in the number of L5s relative to controls, that is, 0.99±0.02 L5s per column compared to 0.83±0.01 L5s per column in controls (Figure 5F–H; p<0.0005, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5F-H.

claim: xgO induce MAPK activity in the most proximal LPCs, resulting in their differentiation and in the production of the feedback inhibitor Aos.
source: Altogether, our data indicate a model in which xgO induce MAPK activity in the most proximal LPCs, resulting in their differentiation and in the production of the feedback inhibitor Aos.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Aos limits further differentiation in the column by fine-tuning the availability of the differentiation signal Spi.
source: In turn, Aos limits further differentiation in the column by fine-tuning the availability of the differentiation signal Spi, which ensures that only one L5 differentiates per column, and determines the final number of neurons in each lamina column.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Each lamina unit or column in the adult is composed of exactly five neurons.
source: In Drosophila, photoreceptors induce their target field, the lamina, thus, establishing retinotopy between the compound eye and the lamina (Huang and Kunes, 1996). Each lamina unit or column in the adult is composed of exactly five neurons; however, columns initially contain six LPCs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is consistent with established knowledge.

claim: The sixth, or 'extra', LPC, invariantly located immediately distal to the differentiating L5 neuron, is fated to die by apoptosis.
source: The sixth, or 'extra', LPC, invariantly located immediately distal to the differentiating L5 neuron, is fated to die by apoptosis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is consistent with the results presented.

claim: The 'extra' LPCs did not differentiate when apoptosis was blocked but generated ectopic L5s when forced to differentiate.
source: These 'extra' LPCs did not differentiate when apoptosis was blocked (Figure 5A and B) but generated ectopic L5s when forced to differentiate (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: It is more likely that the 'extra' cells are specified as L5s, but that other mechanisms restricted their differentiation in Dronc mutants, as other lamina neuron types differentiated normally.
source: Although we cannot rule out that preventing death using Dronc mutants may mis-specify the 'extra' cells and prevent them from differentiating, it is more likely that these 'extra' cells are specified as L5s, but that other mechanisms restricted their differentiation in Dronc mutants, as other lamina neuron types differentiated normally (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: Twice as many LPCs appear to be specified as L5s than undergo differentiation normally.
source: Thus, twice as many LPCs appear to be specified as L5s than undergo differentiation normally, which implies that a selection process to ensure that the correct number of L5s develop is in place.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: A unique strategy for setting neuronal numbers is by regulating how many precursors from a larger pool are induced to differentiate, followed by programmed cell death of the excess precursors.
source: Here, we have defined a unique strategy whereby L5 neuronal numbers are set by regulating how many precursors from a larger pool are induced to differentiate, followed by programmed cell death of the excess precursors.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: xgO secrete at least two ligands (Spi, Col4a1) that activate MAPK signalling in LPCs to induce their differentiation.
source: We showed that a glial population called xgO, which are located proximal to the lamina, secrete at least two ligands (Spi, Col4a1) that activate MAPK signalling in LPCs to induce their differentiation (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Secreted signals from xgO reach the most proximal row of LPCs first due to tissue architecture, and therefore these precursors differentiate first.
source: The tissue architecture is such that secreted signals from the xgO reach the most proximal row of LPCs first, and therefore these precursors differentiate first.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is inferred from the tissue architecture and experimental observations.

claim: Upon differentiation, newly induced L5 neurons secrete the Spi antagonist Aos to limit the available pool of Spi.
source: Upon differentiation, these newly induced neurons secrete the Spi antagonist Aos to limit the available pool of Spi.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by the experimental observations.

claim: The MAPK pathway is not activated in the 'extra' L5 LPCs, preventing them from differentiating into L5 neurons.
source: As a result, the MAPK pathway is not activated in the 'extra' L5 LPCs, preventing them from differentiating into L5 neurons (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by the model shown in Figure 6.

claim: L5 neuronal differentiation in the youngest columns of the lamina proceeds despite Aos secretion by newly induced L5s.
source: Intriguingly, L5 neuronal differentiation in the youngest columns of the lamina proceeds despite Aos secretion by newly induced L5s.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Differentiating L5s express aos at low levels initially and increase expression gradually till it plateaus from column 5 onwards.
source: We noted that differentiating L5s expressed aos (based on aos-lacZ) at low levels initially and increased expression gradually till it plateaued from column 5 onwards (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The delay in high aos expression may enable differentiation of the youngest LPCs, while still inhibiting differentiation of the row immediately distal.
source: This delay in high aos expression may thus enable differentiation of the youngest LPCs, while still inhibiting differentiation of the row immediately distal.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: The structure of the tissue together with feedback from newly induced neurons set neuronal number by limiting which and how many LPCs are induced to differentiate.
source: In sum, the structure of the tissue together with feedback from newly induced neurons set neuronal number by limiting which and, therefore, how many LPCs are induced to differentiate.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: In addition to wrapping glia, another population of glia, the xgO, also receive and relay signals from photoreceptors to induce neuronal differentiation in the lamina.
source: We have shown that in addition to the wrapping glia (Fernandes et al., 2017), another population of glia, the xgO, also receive and relay signals from photoreceptors to induce neuronal differentiation in the lamina (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: This is the first functional role ascribed to xgO.
source: This is the first functional role ascribed to xgO.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the novelty of the findings.

claim: xgO are born from central brain DL1 type II neuroblasts and migrate into the optic lobes to positions below the developing lamina.
source: Remarkably, xgO are born from central brain DL1 type II neuroblasts and migrate into the optic lobes to positions below the developing lamina (Ren et al., 2018; Viktorin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Photoreceptor signals drive wrapping glial morphogenesis and infiltration into the lamina, thus setting the pace of L1-L4 neuronal differentiation.
source: Photoreceptor signals drive wrapping glial morphogenesis and infiltration into the lamina (Franzdóttir et al., 2009), thus setting the pace of L1-L4 neuronal differentiation (Fernandes et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: In the lamina, although the LPCs eliminated by programmed cell death are identifiable and the process stereotyped, it does not appear to be linked to an intrinsic programme.
source: In the lamina, although the LPCs eliminated by programmed cell death are identifiable and the process stereotyped, it does not appear to be linked to an intrinsic programme.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The predictable and stereotyped nature of apoptosis and differentiation are a consequence of stereotyped responses to extrinsic signalling determined by the architecture of the tissue.
source: Rather, the predictable and stereotyped nature of apoptosis and differentiation are a consequence of stereotyped responses to extrinsic signalling determined by the architecture of the tissue.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Stereotyped patterns of apoptosis can arise from extrinsic signalling, suggesting a new mode to reliably pattern development of the nervous system.
source: Thus, our work highlights that stereotyped patterns of apoptosis can arise from extrinsic signalling, suggesting a new mode to reliably pattern development of the nervous system.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: In the lamina, MAPK-induced neuronal differentiation and cell survival appear intimately linked.
source: In the lamina, MAPK-induced neuronal differentiation and cell survival appear intimately linked.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: LPCs that do not activate MAPK signalling sufficiently do not differentiate and are eliminated by apoptosis.
source: LPCs that do not activate MAPK signalling sufficiently do not differentiate and are eliminated by apoptosis, likely through regulation of the proapoptotic factor Head involution defective, which has been described extensively in flies (Bergmann et al., 2002; Bergmann et al., 1998; Kurada and White, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is inferred from the experimental observations and supported by citations.

claim: The xgO-secreted ligands Spi and Col4a1, which activate MAPK, appear to be functioning as differentiation signals as well as trophic factors.
source: Thus, here the xgO-secreted ligands Spi and Col4a1, which activate MAPK, appear to be functioning as differentiation signals as well as trophic factors.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: Col4a1 may perform dual roles by promoting MAPK activity directly through its receptor Ddr, and perhaps also by limiting Spi diffusivity to aid in localising MAPK activation.
source: Col4a1, in particular, may perform dual roles by promoting MAPK activity directly through its receptor Ddr, and perhaps also by limiting Spi diffusivity to aid in localising MAPK activation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is a speculation based on the experimental observations.
